Let the roots of the polynomial be

\[
\alpha^2,\ \beta^2,\ \gamma^2.
\]

By Vieta’s formulas,

\[
\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=\frac n6,
\]

\[
\alpha^2\beta^2+\beta^2\gamma^2+\gamma^2\alpha^2=n-11,
\]

\[
\alpha^2\beta^2\gamma^2=400.
\]

Since \(\alpha^2\beta^2\gamma^2=400\), none of the roots is \(0\), so each root has two square roots.

There are \(8\) sign choices for \((\alpha,\beta,\gamma)\). If there are exactly \(7\) possible values of \(\alpha+\beta+\gamma\), then exactly two sign choices give the same sum.

If two sign choices differed in only one or two signs, that would force either one of \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) to be \(0\), or two of \(\alpha^2,\beta^2,\gamma^2\) to be equal. Both are impossible here. Therefore the two coinciding sign choices must differ in all three signs, meaning their sums are opposites. Since they are equal, that common sum must be \(0\).

So we may choose \(\alpha,\beta,\gamma\) such that

\[
\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0.
\]

Let

\[
q=\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha.
\]

Then

\[
\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=(\alpha+\beta+\gamma)^2-2q=-2q.
\]

Thus

\[
-2q=\frac n6 \implies q=-\frac n{12}.
\]

Also,

\[
(\alpha\beta+\beta\gamma+\gamma\alpha)^2
=\alpha^2\beta^2+\beta^2\gamma^2+\gamma^2\alpha^2
\]

because \(\alpha+\beta+\gamma=0\). Hence

\[
n-11=q^2=\left(-\frac n{12}\right)^2=\frac{n^2}{144}.
\]

So

\[
144(n-11)=n^2
\]

\[
n^2-144n+1584=0.
\]

The discriminant is

\[
144^2-4\cdot 1584=14400=120^2,
\]

so

\[
n=\frac{144\pm 120}{2},
\]

giving

\[
n=132 \quad \text{or} \quad n=12.
\]

It remains to check that \(n=132\) actually works. For \(n=132\),

\[
x^3-22x^2+121x-400=(x-16)(x^2-6x+25),
\]

whose roots are

\[
16,\ 3-4i,\ 3+4i.
\]

These are the squares of

\[
4,\ -2+i,\ -2-i,
\]

whose sum is \(0\). Therefore the eight sign choices give exactly one coincidence, hence exactly \(7\) possible values of \(\alpha+\beta+\gamma\).

Thus the greatest possible integer is

\[
\boxed{132}
\]
